source.title: Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks
source.authors: Kaiming He; Xiangyu Zhang; Shaoqing Ren; Jian Sun

record.tranche_reason: The paper directly compares training behavior under residual shortcut and activation changes, including the original and proposed units.
record.gate_note: Training-loss and training-error comparisons are reported in text or training-curve figures. Test-error tables alone do not measure the claim’s training-error outcome and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures optimization of deep batch-normalized convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, including identity-shortcut ablations and depth-dependent residual-network training difficulties. It tests the residual-network component of V3, but does not reproduce the plain-network depth comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors argue that identity shortcuts and identity after-addition activation enable smooth information propagation, report consistent ablations, and demonstrate successful training of 1001-layer networks. They also attribute part of pre-activation's generalization improvement to regularization.
record.recipe_differences: Compares modifications to residual shortcut and activation recipes against the original ResNet; proposes pre-activation units.
record.method_sensitivity: Shortcut type and scaling, gate bias initialization, activation placement, network depth, and dataset change the reported training behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: A nearly identity gated shortcut gives test error close to the identity-shortcut baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shortcut gate initialization affects CIFAR-10 generalization performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Pre-activation ResNet-164 has slightly higher final training loss and lower test error than its original-unit counterpart.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-activation can improve generalization without reducing final training loss.

record.problems: Training-curve comparisons do not provide numeric training-error values. CIFAR results are reported as medians of 5 runs, but most training-curve uncertainty is not given; the ImageNet ResNet-101 non-identity-shortcut experiments were halted early.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted from test-error-only comparisons in Tables 1–5 because test error does not measure the training-error outcome named in the claim. Figure-only curve values were not estimated.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error is not explicitly established; corrupted-label training and the stated size, stopping, and regularization comparisons are not tested.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and extra student neurons.
Matched plain-network depth degradation, longer-training controls, special initialization of plain tanh networks, and Fixup.
Activation-matched initialization comparisons, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and trainable depth of plain networks.
Stability thresholds, curvature evolution, catapult recovery, and divergence.
BN versus no-BN training-speed and learning-rate comparisons, and Fixup. Rearranging BN within networks that all use BN does not test these comparisons.

missing.what: Original-unit ResNet-200 has lower training error than ResNet-152 on ImageNet, despite worse validation error. This directly records a depth comparison without residual-network training degradation and distinguishes overfitting from optimization failure.
missing.locator: Section 5, Comparisons on ImageNet, paragraph comparing original ResNet-152 and ResNet-200.

missing.what: The original-unit ResNet-164 has only mild initial optimization difficulty and soon trains normally, whereas the difficulty is prominent at 1001 layers. Record this shallower comparison alongside R10 to capture the stated depth dependence.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, Ease of optimization; Figure 6 right compared with Figure 1.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are assigned because this study is explicitly an original source for V3. Shortcut ablations bear on V3's identity-path component but do not independently establish a matched plain-versus-residual depth comparison. CIFAR median accuracy over five runs does not establish uncertainty bands or a five-run median for the plotted training-loss trajectories.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR training with corrupted or random labels; comparisons of small and large models, early stopping, or regularized recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and student width relative to teacher width.
The paper studies residual networks, not the same plain batch-normalized network depth comparison described in the version; it does not test Fixup or special initialization of plain tanh networks.
Initialization comparisons for plain networks, including orthogonal versus Gaussian weights and very deep plain convolutional networks.
Training above a stability limit and sharpness behavior.
Batch normalization versus no normalization as a speed and learning-rate comparison; Fixup.

rows.subject: ResNet-110, original
rows.operation_detail: Train with original identity shortcuts and original residual unit on CIFAR-10.
rows.value: baseline training error; lower than constant scaling and other cited variants in the corresponding comparisons
rows.note: The paper reports this as a reference training-error curve; no numeric training-error value is stated.
rows.check: Figure 3 plots training loss, not training classification error. This is an identity-shortcut control; alone it does not establish the absence of degradation with increasing depth.

source_check.correct: Figure 3 supplies a baseline training-loss curve, not a training-classification-error curve. No numerical training-error rate is stated. For this standalone control, state=cannot_determine for depth-dependent degradation.
source_check.problem: The curve's metric is mislabeled, and the single-depth control alone cannot establish the depth effect.

rows.subject: ResNet-110 with constant scaling (0.5, 0.5)
rows.operation_detail: Train with shortcuts scaled by 0.5 and residual function scaled by 0.5.
rows.baseline: Original ResNet-110 has lower training error
rows.value: Converges, but training error is higher than original ResNet-110
rows.uncertainty: median accuracy of 5 runs; training-error values not stated
rows.note: Table 1 reports test error 12.35%; training comparison is described in text and shown in the curve.
rows.check: The observed comparison favors identity shortcuts over scaled shortcuts. Figure 3(a) plots training loss, although the prose describes higher training error. Calling this partial incorrectly treats a deliberately modified shortcut as failure of the identity-shortcut condition.

rows.subject: ResNet-110 with constant scaling (0.5, 1)
rows.operation_detail: Train with shortcut scaled by 0.5 and unscaled residual function.
rows.value: does not converge well; Table 1 marks it “fail” when test error is higher than 20%
rows.note: The convergence statement bears on training, while the table’s fail threshold is defined using test error.
rows.check: The text reports poor convergence, but the numerical failure criterion is test error above 20%. Neither supplies a readable training-error effect for this setting.

rows.subject: ResNet-110 with exclusive gating, initialized bg=-6
rows.operation_detail: Train with exclusive gates on shortcut and residual paths.
rows.value: training error is higher than original; converges to a solution the authors call poor
rows.uncertainty: median accuracy of 5 runs; training-error values not stated
rows.note: The gate bias was selected by cross-validation; test error is 8.70%.
rows.check: Figure 3(b) plots training loss, not training error. The gated-versus-identity comparison shows an optimization disadvantage of gating; the selected bias is a condition, not a separate result.

source_check.locator_found: Introduction; Section 3.1, Exclusive gating; Table 1; Figure 3(b)

rows.subject: ResNet-110 with shortcut-only gating, initialized bg=0
rows.operation_detail: Gate the shortcut path while leaving F unscaled.
rows.value: higher training error; authors say it causes a poor result
rows.uncertainty: median accuracy of 5 runs; training-error values not stated
rows.note: The paper reports test error 12.86% for this setting.
rows.check: The prose explicitly attributes the poorer result to higher training error; Figure 3(c) itself plots training loss. This is an observed advantage of identity shortcuts over this gated alternative.

rows.subject: ResNet-110 with shortcut-only gating, initialized bg=-6
rows.operation_detail: Gate the shortcut path while leaving F unscaled.
rows.value: result is much closer to the original ResNet-110 baseline
rows.uncertainty: median accuracy of 5 runs; training-error values not stated
rows.note: The text ties the result to the shortcut being nearly identity; test error is 6.91%.
rows.check: The result closer to baseline is test error: 6.91% versus 6.61%. No separate training outcome is reported for this gate bias. Remove this as a training-result row.

rows.subject: ResNet-110 with 1×1 convolutional shortcuts
rows.operation_detail: Replace identity shortcuts with 1×1 convolutional shortcuts.
rows.value: training error becomes higher than original ResNet-110
rows.uncertainty: median accuracy of 5 runs; training-error values not stated
rows.check: The prose reports higher training error, while Figure 3(d) plots training loss. This comparison shows the optimization advantage of identity shortcuts over learned convolutional shortcuts.

rows.subject: ResNet-110 with dropout shortcut
rows.operation_detail: Apply dropout with ratio 0.5 to the identity shortcut output.
rows.value: fails to converge to a good solution
rows.note: Table 1 defines “fail” as test error higher than 20%.
rows.check: Poor convergence is stated, but the reported failure threshold concerns test error. The magnitude of the training-error disadvantage cannot be determined.

rows.subject: ResNet-110 with BN after addition
rows.operation_detail: Place batch normalization after the residual addition.
rows.measure: Training loss at beginning of training
rows.value: difficulties on reducing training loss at the beginning
rows.note: The paper reports test errors of 8.17% for ResNet-110 and 6.61% for the original unit.
rows.check: The reported difficulty is initial training-loss reduction. The shortcut itself remains identity, but BN after addition interrupts the identity propagation path; this qualifies which residual-unit designs ease optimization.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, BN after addition; Table 2; Figure 6 left

rows.subject: ResNet-1001, original Residual Unit
rows.operation_detail: Train original residual units on CIFAR-10.
rows.value: training error is reduced very slowly at the beginning of training
rows.note: The paper gives test error 7.61% for the original and 4.92% for the proposed unit in Table 3.
rows.check: The prose describes slow initial training-error reduction, while Figure 1 plots training loss. This is an early optimization difficulty, not evidence of higher final training classification error.

source_check.correct: The prose reports slow initial training-error reduction; Figure 1 plots training loss. Match the measure to the prose, or describe the plotted initial training-loss reduction without treating it as classification error.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Ease of optimization; Figure 1 caption; Table 3
source_check.problem: The value names training error while the measure names training loss.

rows.subject: ResNet-1001, pre-activation Residual Unit
rows.operation_detail: Train with pre-activation residual units and identity after-addition activation.
rows.value: reduces the training loss very quickly and achieves the lowest loss among the models investigated
rows.note: Text calls this success of optimization; no numeric training error is provided.
rows.check: Rapid loss reduction and the lowest investigated loss establish successful optimization at 1001 layers. They do not provide a numerical final training-error rate.

rows.subject: ResNet-164, pre-activation Residual Unit
rows.operation_detail: Train with full pre-activation residual units.
rows.value: slightly higher training loss at convergence, with lower test error
rows.uncertainty: median of 5 runs; mean±std reported for ResNet-1001 results only
rows.note: This is a qualification: the pre-activation model has higher, not lower, training loss at convergence.
rows.check: Slightly higher final loss after changing activation placement does not establish depth degradation or failure of identity shortcuts. The authors interpret it as regularization; V3 does not predict that pre-activation always lowers final training loss.

rows.subject: ResNet-101 with BN after addition
rows.operation_detail: Train with BN after residual addition on ImageNet.
rows.note: Validation error is also reported as 24.6%/7.5% versus 23.6%/7.1% for original ResNet-101.
rows.check: Higher training loss is explicitly reported, but no training classification-error value is supplied. The 224×224 crop describes validation, not the training-loss measurement.

rows.subject: ResNet-101 with non-identity shortcuts
rows.operation_detail: Train preliminary shortcut variants studied in Figures 2 and 3.
rows.value: obviously higher than the original ResNet at the first learning rate
rows.note: Training was halted due to limited resources.
rows.check: Higher training error of non-identity shortcut variants is explicitly reported relative to the identity baseline. This is an aggregate preliminary result; training stopped during the first learning-rate stage, so it cannot establish final convergence.

relation.reason: Controlled shortcut and activation-placement ablations directly measure residual-network optimization relevant to V3.

tranche.reason: Uses the original ResNet architectures, datasets, training implementation, and training-error/loss comparisons to test shortcut and residual-unit choices.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; no verdicts are listed for this original source. Figures 1, 3 and 6 plot training loss and test error; the plain-network depth comparison is untested here.
